meta.title: Who really said "For whom the bell tolls"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it's genuinely John Donne, from Meditation XVII of his 1624 Devotions upon Emergent Occasions. Not Hemingway, whose 1940 novel borrowed the line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For whom the bell tolls'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely John Donne, from Meditation XVII (Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, 1624). Hemingway's 1940 novel only borrowed it for a title.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1572–1631 · English poet & cleric, later Dean of St Paul’s
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely Donne’s, from the prose “Meditation XVII” of his Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (written 1623, published 1624): “…never send to know for whom the bell tolls; It tolls for thee.” The exact phrase appears verbatim — it is not a later paraphrase.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Devotional prose (not a poem, though often reprinted as verse)
“Nunc lento sonitu dicunt, Morieris” — “Now this bell, tolling softly for another, says to me: Thou must die”

source.excerpt: No man is an Iland, intire of it selfe; every man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine… any mans death diminishes me, because I am involved in Mankinde; And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; It tolls for thee.
trail: The complete Meditation XVII, containing “never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee,” is preserved at Luminarium.
Devotions upon Emergent Occasions was written in December 1623 and published in 1624; Meditation XVII is its most famous section.
Ernest Hemingway’s 1940 novel For Whom the Bell Tolls took its title and epigraph directly from this passage, quoting Donne in his original spelling.
The full 1624 work is public domain and freely readable at Project Gutenberg.
source.excerptNote: Shown in Donne’s original 1624 spelling — the same text Hemingway used as his epigraph. Modernised editions render it “No man is an island… for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”

sourceLink.text: Full text of Meditation XVII at Luminarium

source.rightsNote: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions was first published in 1624 — centuries before the 1931 U.S. public-domain threshold — so both Donne’s original-spelling text and standard modernised renderings of it are firmly in the public domain. Project Gutenberg hosts the full text as public domain in the USA.

author.name: John Donne
author.heading: About John Donne
author.metaLine: 1572–1631 · English metaphysical poet & cleric, Dean of St Paul's Cathedral
author.bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was the leading English metaphysical poet, known for the intellectual wit of works like “The Flea” and the “Holy Sonnets.” After a turbulent early life he took orders in the Church of England and became Dean of St Paul’s in 1621. He wrote the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions in December 1623 while gravely ill, and its Meditation XVII — “No man is an island… for whom the bell tolls” — became his most quoted prose.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is authentically Donne’s — but because of how most people first meet it, credit often lands elsewhere.

items.why: Hemingway’s 1940 novel For Whom the Bell Tolls took both its title and epigraph straight from Donne’s Meditation XVII. Because the novel is so famous, many assume Hemingway coined the phrase — he explicitly did not, and printed Donne’s words as his epigraph.

The line is frequently presented as a Donne poem, but “Meditation XVII” is devotional prose from the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions. Modern anthologies sometimes re-break it into verse lines, which fuels the confusion.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to Donne is correct: the exact wording appears in his 1624 Meditation XVII. Hemingway only borrowed it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Donne wrote the Devotions in December 1623 as he was recovering from a near-fatal illness — probably relapsing fever or typhus. Each of its 23 sections tracks a single day of his sickness through a meditation, an expostulation, and a prayer.

Meditation XVII begins as Donne hears a church bell tolling for a dying neighbour and reflects that the bell may as well be tolling for him — because all people are bound together. The passage turns a memento-mori image into one of the great statements of human interconnectedness.
